# Objective

Before growth curves can be fitted, raw time-lapse images need to be segmented
and the resulting objects tracked over time. `dosefitr` wraps two external
tools for this: [Cellpose](https://www.cellpose.org/) for segmentation and
[TrackMate](https://imagej.net/plugins/trackmate/) (via Fiji) for tracking.
This vignette walks through installing these tools, running the image
processing pipeline, and importing the output back into R.

The code in this vignette is not evaluated when the package is built, as it
depends on external software and local image files.

# Installation

## Cellpose

Cellpose is a Python package and is best installed into its own conda
environment. If you don't already have conda, we recommend
[Miniforge](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge). See https://github.com/mouseland/cellpose for detailed instructions on installation.

`dosefitr` needs the path to the Python executable inside this environment.
With the environment active, you can find it with:

```{bash}
which python
```

On macOS with Miniforge this will look something like
`/Users/<username>/miniforge3/envs/cellpose/bin/python`.

## Fiji and TrackMate

Download [Fiji](https://fiji.sc/) and install it somewhere convenient (for
example, `/Applications/Fiji` on macOS). TrackMate ships with Fiji, so no
further installation is needed. Note the path to the Fiji executable, as
`dosefitr` will need it.

# Example data

An example image is available in the
[`example/` folder](https://github.com/moorezac/dosefitr/tree/main/example/example_data.tiff) of
the `dosefitr` GitHub repository. It is a two-channel time-lapse of 2D cells
imaged every hour for 24 hours, with a brightfield channel and a nuclear stain.
To follow along, download the folder and place it in your working directory.

# Processing images

First, load the package.

```{r echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
library(dosefitr)
```

## Step 2: Cellpose segmentation

`run_cellpose()` takes a directory of merged (or single-channel) images and
writes a `_cp_masks.tif` file alongside each input image. `python` points to
the executable in the conda environment created above.

For the example image, we segment using both the brightfield and nuclear
channels:

```{r cellpose-example}
# Example
path_to_python <- "/Users/<username>/miniforge3/envs/cellpose/bin/python"

dosefitr::run_cellpose(
  input_dir = "example/",
  channels = c(1, 2),
  python = path_to_python
)
```

### Specifying the segmentation channel

Use the `channels` argument to select which channel to segment on (1-based).
For example, to segment on channel 2 only (the nuclear stain in the example
image):

```{r cellpose-channel}
dosefitr::run_cellpose(
  input_dir = "example/",
  channels = 2,
  python = "/Users/<username>/miniforge3/envs/cellpose/bin/python"
)
```

### Passing extra Cellpose arguments

Any additional Cellpose command-line arguments can be forwarded via
`cellpose_args`. They are passed verbatim to the Cellpose CLI. For example, to
set a fixed object diameter of 30 pixels:

```{r cellpose-args}
dosefitr::run_cellpose(
  input_dir = "example/",
  channels = 2,
  python = "/Users/<username>/miniforge3/envs/cellpose/bin/python",
  cellpose_args = c("--diameter", "30")
)
```

## Step 3: TrackMate cell tracking

`run_trackmate()` merges the Cellpose masks with their source images, generates
a TrackMate macro, and runs it via the Fiji command line. Track files (`.xml`)
and spot tables (`_spots.csv`) are written to a `trackmate/` folder inside
`input_dir`.

```{r trackmate-example}
# Example
path_to_fiji <- "/Applications/Fiji/fiji"

dosefitr::run_trackmate(
  input_dir = "example/",
  fiji_path = path_to_fiji
)
```

### Tightening linking parameters

The default linking distances are conservative (200 pixels). For densely packed
cells or slower-moving populations you will typically want to tighten these:

```{r trackmate-tight}
dosefitr::run_trackmate(
  input_dir = "example/",
  fiji_path = path_to_fiji,
  frame_linking_max_distance = 50,
  gap_closing_max_distance = 50,
  gap_closing_max_frame_gap = 2
)
```

### Cell division (track splitting)

Track splitting is enabled by default, which allows TrackMate to detect cell
division events. You can tune the maximum distance at which a split is
accepted:

```{r trackmate-split}
dosefitr::run_trackmate(
  input_dir = "example/",
  fiji_path = path_to_fiji,
  allow_track_splitting = TRUE,
  track_splitting_max_distance = 20
)
```

To disable division detection entirely (for example, for non-dividing
populations):

```{r trackmate-nosplit}
dosefitr::run_trackmate(
  input_dir = "example/",
  fiji_path = path_to_fiji,
  allow_track_splitting = FALSE
)
```

### Verbose output

Set `verbose = TRUE` to print the full TrackMate configuration and the Fiji
command to the console before running, which is useful for debugging:

```{r trackmate-verbose}
dosefitr::run_trackmate(
  input_dir = "example/",
  fiji_path = path_to_fiji,
  verbose = TRUE
)
```

## Running on an HPC

`run_cellpose()` and `run_trackmate()` are convenient for small experiments,
but they process images one at a time on your local machine. For a full plate,
this can take many hours. If you have access to a high-performance computing
(HPC) cluster, it is much faster to use the scripts provided with the package. You can find where they are with:

```{r hpc-scripts}
hpc_scripts <- system.file("python", package = "dosefitr")
list.files(hpc_scripts, full.names = TRUE)
```

# Importing and summarising data

`import_trackmate()` reads the TrackMate spot files into a named list of data
frames, one per well. Where a well ID can't be found in the filename, the
filename itself is used as the name instead.

```{r import}
data <- dosefitr::import_trackmate(
  spot_path = "example/trackmate/"
)

data$example_data
```

If timestamps were exported alongside the images, pass their directory to
`datetime_path` to join acquisition times onto each frame.

`summarise_trackmate()` collapses the per-spot data into per-frame summaries
for each well, such as the number of spots and their mean radius. Here we have
no timestamps, so we summarise by frame. As the example image was acquired
hourly, each frame corresponds to one hour.

```{r summarise}
data_sum <- dosefitr::summarise_trackmate(
  spot_list = data,
  datetime_column = "frame"
)
```

We can then plot these summaries over time. Mean radius gives a measure of
object size:

```{r plot-radius}
ggplot2::ggplot(
  data_sum$example_data,
  ggplot2::aes(frame, mean_radius)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  theme_dosefitr()
```

And the number of spots tracks how many objects are detected in each frame:

```{r plot-spots}
ggplot2::ggplot(
  data_sum$example_data,
  ggplot2::aes(frame, num_spots)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  theme_dosefitr()
```

sessionInfo()
